reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: A male factor contributes to roughly half of couples presenting with infertility, so both partners should be evaluated in parallel from the outset
Semen analysis is the cornerstone investigation and should be repeated because of considerable biological variability before conclusions are drawn
Abnormalities are described in terms of sperm concentration, motility, and morphology, with azoospermia, oligozoospermia, and asthenozoospermia denoting the main patterns
Causes are grouped into pre-testicular (hypothalamic-pituitary and hormonal), testicular (primary spermatogenic failure), and post-testicular (obstruction or ejaculatory disorders)
Endocrine evaluation with gonadotrophins and testosterone helps localise the problem; low gonadotrophins suggest a central cause whereas high FSH indicates primary testicular failure
Varicocele is a common and potentially correctable cause, and reversible contributors such as heat, smoking, alcohol, obesity, and certain drugs should be sought
Azoospermia should be characterised as obstructive or non-obstructive, since surgical sperm retrieval with assisted reproduction can achieve fatherhood in many cases
Genetic evaluation, including karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing, is indicated in severe oligozoospermia or non-obstructive azoospermia
reference.pathophysiology: Male fertility depends on the integrity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, on spermatogenesis within the seminiferous tubules driven by FSH and intratesticular testosterone, and on an unobstructed ductal system allowing sperm transport and ejaculation. Pre-testicular disease reflects deficient gonadotrophin stimulation (hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism from pituitary or hypothalamic disorders, hyperprolactinaemia, or exogenous androgen use). Testicular causes include genetic conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, prior orchitis, chemotherapy or radiation, and varicocele-related impairment of the testicular thermal and vascular environment. Post-testicular causes include congenital absence or acquired obstruction of the vas deferens, ejaculatory duct obstruction, retrograde ejaculation, and antisperm antibodies. The final common pathway is a reduction in the number or function of sperm reaching the oocyte.
additionalDifferentials: Primary testicular failure including Klinefelter syndrome
Obstructive azoospermia including congenital absence of the vas deferens
Exogenous androgen or anabolic steroid use suppressing spermatogenesis
additionalInvestigations: Repeated semen analysis performed to standard laboratory criteria
Hormonal profile including FSH, LH, testosterone, and prolactin
Scrotal examination and ultrasound to detect varicocele or obstruction
Karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis in severe cases
Post-ejaculatory urinalysis when retrograde ejaculation is suspected
redFlags: Azoospermia requiring prompt distinction between obstructive and non-obstructive causes
Signs of a pituitary mass such as visual field loss or headache with low gonadotrophins
Bilateral testicular atrophy or gynaecomastia suggesting significant endocrine or genetic disease
A testicular mass discovered during fertility evaluation, raising concern for malignancy
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the cause; hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and obstruction are often correctable, varicocele repair may improve parameters in selected men, and even severe spermatogenic failure can frequently be overcome by surgical sperm retrieval combined with assisted reproductive techniques.
pitfalls: Investigating and treating only the female partner while overlooking male factor contribution
Drawing conclusions from a single abnormal semen analysis without repeat testing
Missing exogenous androgen or anabolic steroid use as a reversible cause of azoospermia
Failing to offer genetic counselling before assisted reproduction in men with genetic causes
